Opened arXiv:2511.09803v2 ("Retrieval as a Decision: Training-Free Adaptive Gating for Efficient RAG", Yufeng Wang, Lu Wei, Haibin Ling) via WebFetch of both the abstract page and the full HTML (arxiv.org/html/2511.09803v2). Every load-bearing element of the claim matches the source verbatim:
- TARG = "Training-free Adaptive Retrieval Gating"; described as a single-shot policy deciding when to retrieve using only a short no-context draft, "requires no additional training or auxiliary heads" — confirms "training-free adaptive retrieval GATE."
- Draft prefix: "we decode a short prefix from the base prompt B(q), compute U(q) once", "k=20 used by default (best cost/quality balance)" — confirms k=20.
- Mean token entropy: H_t = −∑_j π_{t,j} log π_{t,j}; U_ent(k) = (1/k)∑_{t=1}^k H_t — confirmed.
- Margin: g_t = ℓ_{t,(1)} − ℓ_{t,(2)} (top-1 vs top-2 logit gap); U_mar(k;β) = (1/k)∑ φ(g_t) with default φ(z) = exp(−z/β), default β = 3 — confirms "U_mar = mean exp(-gap/beta), beta=3 recommended default."
- Small-N variance: d_t = 1 − max_j p̂_t(j); U_var(k,N) = (1/k)∑ d_t across N stochastic prefixes (default N=5, T=0.7) — confirms "small-N prefix variance."
- Decision rule: "retrieve(q) ⟺ U(q) > τ" — confirms "retrieves iff U>tau."
- Threshold calibration: budget mode "To hit a retrieval budget ρ ∈ [0,1], pick τ = F_U^{−1}(1−ρ)"; accuracy mode "select τ that maximizes dev accuracy" — confirms both calibration options exactly, both training-free/dev-set based.
The only non-source element is the editorial framing "the closest existing instantiation of our tau* layer," which is the writer's own positioning about their project, not a claim about the paper's content, and is therefore neither confirmed nor refutable by the source. All verifiable technical assertions are accurate.

Source opened: arXiv 2511.09803v2, "Retrieval as a Decision," which introduces TARG = Training-free Adaptive Retrieval Gating. Two independent fetches corroborate the claim.

(1) Ensembling ablation — CONFIRMED nearly verbatim. Full text Section 3.2: "We also explored simple aggregation of the three gates (e.g., normalizing each U to [0,1] and averaging). On a dev split, these ensembles did not yield consistent improvements over the best single gate once τ and k are tuned; the combined scores behave like re-parameterized margin gates while introducing extra weights to calibrate. For simplicity and robustness, we therefore present each gate separately and recommend Margin as a default." The claim's phrasing ("ensembling ... did NOT consistently beat the best single gate once tau and k are tuned") maps directly onto "did not yield consistent improvements over the best single gate once τ and k are tuned."

(2) Ships single-signal, margin default — CONFIRMED. Independently supported by the abstract: "the margin signal is a robust default (entropy compresses as backbones sharpen), with small-N variance offering a conservative, budget-first alternative." The three signals are mean token entropy, a margin signal (top-1/top-2 logit gap via a monotone link), and small-N variance across stochastic prefixes. τ = retrieval decision threshold (retrieve if U(q) > τ, calibrated via empirical CDF to hit a budget); k = prefix length in tokens (default k=20).

(3) The trailing framing — "in tension with the multi-signal literature" and "a concrete ablation we can re-test on the speech-omni" — is the claim author's own editorial/forward-looking interpretation, not an assertion attributed to the paper, so it needs no correction; it is a reasonable characterization (the paper's own reading is milder: the combined scores "behave like re-parameterized margin gates"). The load-bearing factual content of the claim is accurate and well-sourced.

Opened arxiv.org/html/2510.19471 ("Re-evaluating MBR Decoding for ASR"). CONFIRMED parts: (a) Selection rule verbatim — "y^ = argmax_{y∈H} (1/N) Σ_{y'∈H} u(y,y')". (b) Sampling — "epsilon sampling ... with ϵ=0.01 and a temperature set to 1.0", tested at N=4,8,16,32,64 (up to 64). (c) No gold reference at inference — MBR compares hypotheses to each other, not to references. (d) "Surprisingly, with only four to eight samples, MBR decoding outperforms beam search." (e) Quadratic in sample count. REFUTED/MISSTATED parts: (1) The "~20–35% relative WER reduction" range is unsupported. Actual reductions are strongly condition-dependent, spanning roughly ~5% (ReazonSpeech SNR=0dB, 0.305→0.291 ≈ 4.6%) to ~50%+ (some Whisper models), with the flagship whisper-large-v3 on clean LibriSpeech only 0.036→0.029 ≈ 19% — below the claimed 20% floor. The paper states NO "20–35%" summary range. (2) The ROVER reduction is not "exactly": the paper says "When the utility function is a token-level edit metric (such as WER or Levenshtein distance), MBR reduces to A FORM OF ROVER-style majority voting" — explicitly a form of, not exact equivalence. (3) Complexity is stated precisely as O(UN²+GN) (with U the utility-call cost), plus a faster O(UN log N + GN) variant noted — the claim's loose "O(N²) in the utility" garbles this.
correction: Two quantitative/qualitative specifics are wrong. (1) WER reduction: the paper does NOT report a "~20–35%" range; gains are highly condition-dependent, roughly ~5% up to ~50%+, and the flagship whisper-large-v3 on LibriSpeech is only ~19% (below the claimed lower bound). Replace "~20–35% relative WER reduction" with "condition-dependent WER reductions ranging from a few percent up to ~50%, with no single summary range asserted." (2) ROVER: MBR reduces to "a FORM OF ROVER-style majority voting" when the utility is a token-edit metric — NOT "exactly." Drop "exactly." Also, the complexity is precisely O(UN²+GN) (quadratic in the number of samples N, with U per-utility cost; a faster O(UN log N + GN) variant exists), which is more accurate than "O(N²) in the utility." The formula, epsilon-sampling parameters (ε=0.01, T=1.0, up to 64 samples), no-gold-reference property, and the 4–8-sample emergence are all accurate as stated.

Source opened: arxiv.org/abs/2502.18581 (abstract) + full paper arxiv.org/html/2502.18581v1. CONFIRMED elements: (1) self-certainty = KL divergence of the token probability distribution from uniform — exact formula Self-certainty = -1/(nV) ∑_{i=1}^{n} ∑_{j=1}^{V} log(V·p(j|x,y<i)), which the paper states equals the KL divergence between a uniform distribution and the predicted token distribution (up to an additive constant vs. cross-entropy); (2) "aggregated across multiple samples" (abstract); (3) combined with Borda voting, v(r)=(N−r+1)^p, ranking responses by self-certainty (p=0 → majority voting); (4) "without requiring external reward models," reward-free, no gold answer needed; (5) abstract point 3 and LiveCodeBench experiments show it "generalizes to open-ended tasks where traditional self-consistency methods fall short / is inapplicable." REFUTED element: the claim says KL of the "token TOP-K logprob distribution." Two separate fetches confirm the inner summation runs over j=1…V (the ENTIRE vocabulary), and the paper does NOT define or primarily use any top-k-truncated version of the metric.
correction: Replace "token top-k logprob distribution" with "full next-token probability distribution over the entire vocabulary V." Self-certainty is the KL divergence from uniform computed over ALL vocabulary tokens (sum j=1…V), not a top-k subset — the paper never uses a top-k-truncated variant as its metric. Every other component of the claim (KL-from-uniform, aggregation across N samples, Borda voting, no gold answer / no external reward model, generalization to open-ended tasks where self-consistency fails) is accurate.

Source opened and confirmed real: arXiv 2603.21172, "Entropy Alone is Insufficient for Safe Selective Prediction in LLMs" (Phillips, Gustafsson, Wu, Thakur, Clifton; submitted 2026-03-22). Verified via WebFetch of the abstract and the HTML body.

CONFIRMED parts of the claim:
(a) "Entropy alone is insufficient for SAFE selective prediction" = the paper's exact title/thesis. Abstract: it identifies "a model-dependent failure mode of entropy-based uncertainty methods that leads to unreliable abstention behaviour."
(b) Combining a signal with entropy improves the risk-coverage curve — abstract: the combined score "generally improves both the risk-coverage trade-off and calibration performance relative to entropy-only baselines."
(d) The evaluation protocol claim is well supported: body reports risk-coverage curves ("coverage" and "selective risk"), "Excess Area Under the Risk-Coverage Curve (E-AURC)", and "AUROC and AUPRC for hallucination detection" (plus Target Calibration Error). So risk-coverage + E-AURC + AUROC-for-correctness is accurate.

REFUTED / INACCURATE part (load-bearing): the specific fusion recipe. The claim says the paper fuses "entropy + margin + semantic entropy + self-consistency." The paper does NOT. Its proposed score is "a two-feature logistic regression over u_ent(x) and u_pc(x)" — i.e., ENTROPY + a Probability-of-Correctness (PC) / correctness probe only. Semantic Entropy (SE) and the Semantic Entropy Probe (SEP) appear only as BASELINES, not as fused components; "margin" and "self-consistency" are not the combined signals at all. The abstract corroborates: "combining entropy scores with a correctness probe signal."

OVERREACH part: "no single signal reliably flags incorrect LLM outputs across tasks/models" overgeneralizes. The paper's negative claim is scoped specifically to entropy (a "model-dependent" failure in a "confidently wrong regime" of low-entropy hallucinations); it does not establish that every single signal fails. Also "substantially improves" overstates the paper's "generally improves."
correction: The high-level thesis and the evaluation-protocol description are correct, but the fusion recipe is wrong and must be corrected. The paper does NOT fuse "entropy + margin + semantic entropy + self-consistency." Its actual proposed gate is a two-feature logistic regression combining just two signals: token/sequence ENTROPY (u_ent) and a Probability-of-Correctness / correctness PROBE (u_pc). Semantic entropy (SE) and the semantic-entropy probe (SEP) are evaluated only as baselines, and margin / self-consistency are not used. Restate as: "the paper fuses entropy with a trained correctness (probability-of-correctness) probe." Also narrow "no single signal reliably flags incorrect outputs across tasks/models" to the paper's actual, entropy-specific finding (a model-dependent 'confidently-wrong' low-entropy failure mode), and soften "substantially improves" to "generally improves." The metrics claim (risk-coverage curves + E-AURC + AUROC, also AUPRC and Target Calibration Error) is accurate.

evidence: Source opened and verified at the primary level (fetched abstract page, HTML, and downloaded the 765 KB PDF, then extracted its text). Paper confirmed: "Re-evaluating Minimum Bayes Risk Decoding for Automatic Speech Recognition," Yuu Jinnai, TMLR 05/2026, arXiv:2510.19471 — genuinely an ASR/ST paper using sample-based MBR decoding on Whisper. The load-bearing factual assertions in the claim are CONFIRMED verbatim from the Method section: "We use the BLEU score ... as the utility function of MBR. We do not use WER (CER) as the utility function because MBR decoding is known to inflate the score used as the utility function which may not accurately reflect a model's true capabilities (Freitag et al., 2022; Kovacs et al., 2024)." Corroborated by two table captions ("MBR using SentBERT may lead to inflate SemDist scores that do not accurately reflect a model's true capabilities"; Table 10: "BLEU scores are used as the utility function for MBR decoding, which may lead to artificially inflated scores that do not accurately reflect a model's true capabilities"). So: (a) the paper DOES deliberately avoid WER/CER as the utility, and (b) the stated reason IS that MBR inflates whatever score it optimizes. That much is exact. The claim is downgraded to PARTIAL only for its interpretive tail.
correction: Two nuances the claim overstates. (1) The paper does not present MBR utility inflation as its own finding — it states it as ESTABLISHED prior knowledge ("is known to inflate"), citing Freitag et al. 2022 and Kovacs et al. 2024. It is real and correctly cited, but this paper is a downstream user of the result, not its source. (2) More importantly, the framing "a concrete instance of the over-optimization edge that a budget/regularization constraint must bound" is the claimant's own theory-side extrapolation, NOT what the paper does. The paper's actual mitigation for the inflation is METRIC DECOUPLING — choosing a utility (BLEU) that differs from the evaluation metric (WER/CER) so the reported score is not the optimized score. It uses no budget cap or regularization/KL term to bound over-optimization; the N=64 sample count is a fixed compute setting justified nowhere as a convergence constraint. So the paper supports "the over-optimization/Goodhart edge is real," but it does NOT validate the specific remedy (budget N* / regularization β) the project's convergence-theory track invokes. Cite this paper as evidence the edge exists and that practitioners avoid optimizing the eval metric directly — not as evidence that a budget/regularization constraint is the mechanism that bounds it.

Opened arxiv 2502.18581 ("Scalable Best-of-N Selection... via Self-Certainty") via arxiv.org/html/2502.18581 plus corroborating searches. The claim's FRAMING is right but its DEFINING FORMULA is wrong.

CONFIRMED sub-claims:
- Training-free, gold-free, reward-model-free Best-of-N selector using only the model's own output distribution: paper states it estimates response quality "without requiring external reward models." 
- Rank N candidates, pick the max self-certainty (best-of-N).
- Cheap / effectively free at generation: "almost no computational overhead, as the token distribution is generated alongside the tokens during inference."

REFUTED — the core mathematical definition. The paper defines self-certainty as a KL-divergence-from-uniform DISTRIBUTIONAL measure that sums over the ENTIRE vocabulary V at every position: Self-Certainty = -(1/nV) Σ_{i=1..n} Σ_{j=1..V} log(V·p(j | x, y_<i)) (some renderings normalize by 1/n vs 1/nV, but both sum over all V). The claim instead defines it as the mean token log-probability SC(y)=(1/|y|)Σ log P(t_i|t_<i) — i.e., the log-prob of only the sampled tokens (perplexity/likelihood). That is a DIFFERENT quantity, and critically it is the exact BASELINE the paper argues against: the paper treats perplexity/mean-log-prob as a separate baseline and finds it substantially worse ("negative perplexity fails to clearly separate correct from incorrect outputs"; perplexity plateaus/declines after N≈16 while KL-based self-certainty keeps improving to N=64). So the claim mislabels the method as the very metric the paper shows is inferior.

REFUTED/UNSUPPORTED — "2-5x fewer tokens than majority voting for comparable/better accuracy." The paper reports NO such token multiplier (the 1-3x / 2-5x figures come from related but different work, e.g. 2502.00511). Moreover, pure self-certainty Best-of-N UNDERPERFORMS self-consistency (majority voting) at identical N on math tasks (GSM8K/MATH/LiveBench-Math); it only matches/beats self-consistency when combined via Borda voting or on open-ended tasks. So "comparable/better accuracy" is false for the pure BoN variant on convergent-answer tasks.

PARTIAL — the "confidence not correctness (high-prob can be wrong)" limitation. Directionally fine (paper notes vulnerability to artificially inflated confidence and inferiority to majority voting on convergent tasks), but the paper's thesis is that self-certainty is a BETTER-calibrated signal than raw probability, so "high-prob can be wrong" more precisely critiques the mean-log-prob metric the claim wrongly attributes to it.
correction: Fix the formula: Self-Certainty is NOT mean token log-probability. It is the average KL divergence from a uniform distribution over the full vocabulary — Self-Certainty(y) = -(1/nV) Σ_{i=1..n} Σ_{j=1..V} log(V · p(j | x, y_<i)) — computed over the ENTIRE predicted distribution at each step (not just the sampled token). Mean-log-prob / perplexity is a separate, weaker baseline the paper explicitly shows underperforms self-certainty. Consequently, "one forward pass per candidate (or free if logprobs are captured)" is only correct if you capture the FULL per-step distribution, not just sampled-token logprobs. Drop or heavily qualify "2-5x fewer tokens than majority voting for comparable/better accuracy": the paper reports no such multiplier, and pure self-certainty Best-of-N actually underperforms self-consistency at equal N on math benchmarks (it needs Borda-style vote integration to match/beat it, and its clear win is on open-ended tasks where self-consistency doesn't apply). Keep as-is: training-free, gold-free, reward-model-free, rank-N-pick-max, negligible generation-time cost.
